1:
The first verse contradicts the third. The heading places the word in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, but the messengers are sent to kings who had come to Zedekiah, who did not reign until eleven years later. John Gill sets out the options: some attach the verse to the previous chapter, which the word saying at its end forbids; some think it a copyist’s error, and the Syriac and Arabic do read Zedekiah, though he was Josiah’s brother; others hold the prophecy was given then but concealed. Adam Clarke calls it most evident that the prophecy was delivered about the fourth year of Zedekiah, and reports three manuscripts reading Zedekiah. Charles Ellicott says the Hebrew text has perpetuated an error due probably to the transcriber or first editor of the collected prophecies, and places it about the middle of Zedekiah’s reign. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same verdict differently, arguing that the three chapters are closely connected and the date here irreconcilable with that of the next, so the name in the heading is erroneous. Matthew Henry allows that if a mistake is admitted anywhere it should be here; but he prefers a solution from a scholar of his day, that the yokes were made in Jehoiakim’s time as a token of the subjection which began then, and sent to the neighbouring kings later under Zedekiah. John Calvin defends the received text, holding that the beginning of a reign extends over the whole of it while prosperous, and that the prophecy was committed to the prophet but not to be promulgated at once—done for his own sake, that he might perform his office with more alacrity, knowing that no one thought the thing could happen.

The sign itself is a yoke worn by the prophet. Gill and Clarke describe it, the yokes of wood and the bonds thongs binding them so that the yoke might not slip from the neck. Ellicott places it in a tradition of symbolic prediction, with an earlier prophet who walked naked and barefoot as precedent, and asks us to realise the far more vivid impression made by the prophet appearing at once a captive slave and a beast of burden, than by simply warning of a coming subjugation. He quotes a Roman poet to the effect that things heard stir the soul less than what the eye sees acted out; from a later chapter, he adds, the command was obeyed quite literally. John Wesley notes that the prophet was to put one yoke on his own neck, to be a type both to his own people and to the nations named.

Why the ambassadors were in Jerusalem is explained most fully by Calvin. When the neighbouring kings saw that the Babylonian would spare none of them they began to join forces; each had at first consulted his own advantage and seen no need of mutual help, which was how the Chaldeans easily overcame them while disunited, until experience taught them that none could sustain the contest without a confederacy. So the kings of Tyre and Sidon and Moab and Ammon offered their forces to the king of Judah, who promised help in return. This was a new occasion of confidence to the Jews, who gathered courage to resist; and God, Calvin says, designed the message chiefly for Zedekiah and the Jews, since these embassies might have emboldened them to despise all prophecy. Ellicott adds that the princes are named in the same order as in a prophecy delivered fifteen years earlier, that they were encouraged by difficulties which seemed to delay the Chaldean triumph, and that the prophet is to tell them their efforts are in vain, the supremacy of Babylon being for the time part of God’s order for chastising the nations. Wesley notes only that these nations were neighbours to the Jews, their princes keeping ambassadors resident in Jerusalem.
4:
The message is entrusted to the ambassadors themselves, and John Calvin notices how odd that is. They might have refused, and with indignation—who art thou to command us, and do you think us so mad as to threaten our own kings for your sake, and tell them they are shortly to become servants of the Chaldean? They might have treated the prophet with derision. But the whole thing, Calvin says, was done for the sake of Zedekiah and the people, to dissipate the vain splendour by which he saw them deceived; for they reckoned they had high mountains set against the Chaldean army—on what side can they assail us, since the kings of Tyre and Sidon and Moab and Ammon are on our side, who rule widely and whose cities are impregnable? Calvin also corrects the rendering of the verse, holding that the Hebrew will not admit the usual transposition and requires command them as to their masters rather than command them to say to their masters. John Gill keeps to the authority behind it, that the prophet is sent to speak in a very high strain, having his orders from a greater master than the messengers had. Charles Ellicott finds a special force in the divine title as addressed to nations who were not worshippers of that God: they, with their hosts of earth, were setting themselves against the Lord of the hosts of heaven and earth alike.

The ground of the claim is creation. Ellicott notes that the pronoun is emphatic, corrects two phrases—on the face of the earth, and it seemed meet to my eyes—and observes that the stretched-out arm is characteristic of Deuteronomy, one of many traces of that book’s influence on this prophet’s language. The whole preface, he says, rises to a height of rhythmic loftiness not common in these writings, and asserts that the Creator of the material world is also ruler over the kingdoms of the earth. Adam Clarke and Gill state the same argument more briefly, Gill grounding God’s right to dispose of the earth and all in it on his having made and his continuing to sustain it. Calvin agrees that the pronouns are emphatic and would render the verb as future—I will give it to whom it shall seem right in my eyes—taking the fifth verse as a general declaration and the sixth as the particular determination, that these lands have been given to one man.

Calvin also uses the passage to state a rule about signs. The spectacle would have been unmeaning had the prophet only put the yoke on his neck and added no instruction, for all signs are as it were dead unless life is given them by the word; an image avails little, and whatever signs are set before our eyes are frivolous if no doctrine is added as their life. He turns this against a church of his own day which, he says, amuses the minds of the people with many signs while conveying no doctrine, and concludes that such things are mere figments attended with no profit. Ellicott suggests the stress laid on the beasts may connect with the nations’ resistance to levies made by Babylonian officers on their horses and cattle, or with the conquerors’ claim to use the subdued land as a hunting-ground, as depicted on Assyrian sculptures. Calvin reads them as an argument to shame: the very beasts, tigers and wolves and lions, shall know by a hidden instinct that this king is their master, and if they obey him because God raised him to that dignity, how great must be the stupidity of men in not acknowledging what the beasts understand? Clarke states the conclusion without ornament, that these kingdoms are at God’s sovereign disposal and that for the punishment of their rulers and people he gives them for a time into one hand.
7:
The succession named here invites a count of Babylonian kings, and the count is disputed. Adam Clarke takes the words strictly, naming the son and the grandson and calling the whole literally fulfilled. John Wesley gives the same two names and dates the term at seventy years. John Calvin reports the difficulty. Most think there were only two successors of the founder’s own posterity; others name five. Those who allow three appeal to this verse, since only a son and a grandson are named, but Calvin thinks that no sufficient reason, and follows the more commonly received view that the last king of Babylon, slain by Cyrus, was the third from the first, two others having held regal power for a time without being of that line. Charles Ellicott weighs the phrase itself rather than the history. It may have meant that this was the farthest limit of the dynasty, as defined by the seventy years named earlier; but the same phrase elsewhere points rather to an undefined prolongation, subject only to an appointed limit. He gives the succession as four names rather than three, and notes that the whole verse is missing from the Greek, perhaps because the translators thought the son’s son inconsistent with history as they read it.

The last clause of the verse is read as pointing both ways. Ellicott corrects the rendering—not shall serve themselves of him but shall make him to serve—and observes that in the nature of the case the pronoun refers to whoever is king of Babylon at the time, the confederacy of nations that would overthrow the monarchy being described more fully in a later chapter. The words, he says, were clearly meant to point in two directions at once: they warn the nations not to resist the Chaldean king now, and they warn the king not to think he is founding a dynasty of long duration. Calvin draws the same lesson from the phrase about the time of his land. That time was determined by heaven; as a limit is fixed for each of us beyond which none can pass, so we ought to judge of kingdoms, the life and death of every kingdom being in God’s hand and at his will. He allows that the phrase should not be confined to the first king, since his grandson represented him, so that the time may aptly be called his when God put an end to his power. John Gill limits the scope of the promise, that all nations means all those named, though others were tributary too, and not every nation under heaven.

The threat attached to the decree is explained by Calvin as a concession to slowness. It ought to have been enough to say that this king was God’s servant to subdue Judea, but since it was hard for the Jews to receive an enemy, the threatening had to be added—see what you do, for you cannot be stronger than God. The threat was already implied in what went before, but men are tardy to learn when a false impression has preoccupied their minds; the Jews would have gone on evading had their obduracy not been broken by this word. Calvin adds an argument from the lesser to the greater: if God would so severely punish the pride of the Gentiles for withdrawing from that yoke, the Jews ought to have dreaded a heavier vengeance, having been warned by a prophet and knowing that what befell them was a righteous judgment on their sins. Ellicott corrects one word in the sentence, preferring I will visit to I will punish, and observes that the three forms of punishment go naturally together, appearing elsewhere with a fourth added as the sore judgments of God. Gill glosses the refusal to serve as declining to submit and become tributary when the king approached and besieged them.
9:
Five kinds of diviner are named, and the list is significant. Charles Ellicott suggests the catalogue may have its ground in the fact that each name was characteristic of one of the five nations addressed. He glosses them in turn: the idea in prophet is full-flowing utterance; in diviners, the casting of lots; in enchanters, secret arts; in sorcerers, muttered spells. The confederacy, he adds, was sustained in its rebellion by a unanimity of prediction from men of all these classes, every oracle being tuned in favour of resistance. Adam Clarke works through the same five from their roots: the dreamers from a word meaning to break in pieces, since a dream consists of broken fragments out of which interpreters patch a meaning; the enchanters from the word for a cloud, so that they divine by the flight and shape of clouds; the sorcerers from a verb meaning to discover, finders-out of hidden things. Every nation had such persons, gladly encouraged by the multitude and many of them mere apes of the true prophets; man knows he is short-sighted, feels pain at the uncertainty of the future, and wishes his doubts resolved. John Calvin reports two derivations for the fourth name, either observers of stated times who promise a happy issue on this or that day, or diviners by the stars; he sets out one scholar’s five definitions and notes that another makes the second a general term. John Gill notes that these words are not addressed to the Jews but are part of what the messengers were to say to their own masters, those nations having their prophets too.

Calvin insists that the passage was designed for the Jews, since what follows could not be applied to heathen nations; what was said of augurs and magicians must be understood of the impostors who under the name of prophets deceived that miserable people. He reconstructs the objection made against the prophet—art thou alone to be believed, and how dost thou prove that what thou teachest is from heaven?—and observes that the ungodly usually clamour so. He applies the same complaint to a church of his own day which covers every abomination by the plea that Scripture is obscure and controversy uncertain, so that nothing is believed but what the church has decreed. The prophet was met with such clamours and persevered nonetheless.

The promise attached to submission is where the chapter turns. Keil and Delitzsch supply the political reasoning: the great conquerors of that region contented themselves at first with subjecting the vanquished and imposing tribute, destroying kingdoms and deporting populations only where resistance was stubborn. Zedekiah and the ambassadors might have learnt this from the conqueror’s conduct after the earlier capture of Jerusalem, had they not been infatuated by a lying spirit whose predictions suited the wishes of the natural heart. Ellicott says the prophet speaks of what he foresees will result from the rebellion as though the soothsayers intended it, treating them like the lying spirit that persuaded a king to go up to battle and perish; the advice given here to the five nations, he notes, is addressed specifically to Judah in the next verse and repeated more fully after the deportation. Calvin reads the mention of the nations as a way of touching the Jews: if God will spare heathen nations to whom he has promised nothing, what may his chosen people expect—and if he punishes nations that err in darkness, what will become of a people who knowingly resist his judgments? Their obstinacy was mad impiety, since knowing this king to be the executioner of God’s vengeance, to exempt themselves from his power was to fight with God. He notes finally a play in the Hebrew, the same verb meaning both to serve and to cultivate, so that subjection and the tilling of their own land are set against each other in one word.
12:
The message is now turned on Judah itself, and everyone marks the shift. John Calvin says this verse proves that all that went before was spoken especially to the chosen people, since the prophet was not sent as a teacher to the Moabites and Tyrians but had his limits prescribed. He draws out what the prophetic office is: its doctrine is higher than all earthly elevations, and though the prophet was one of the people and did not exempt himself from the king’s authority or pretend to be released from the laws, when he exercised his spiritual jurisdiction in God’s name he spared neither king nor counsellors. Calvin contrasts this with the clergy of his own day, who boast of an immunity from ordinary law which he calls a licence to live in wickedness. He notes that the prophet skilfully assailed the king first, having been sent to him, and yet addressed him in the plural, because the greater part of the people depended on their king’s will. Charles Ellicott observes that there was a party of resistance in Judah too, trusting in delusive prophecies of the overthrow of the Chaldean monarchy, and hears the prophet pleading earnestly with them in the question that follows. Keil and Delitzsch explain the plural the same way, that in and along with the king his people are addressed. John Gill notes only that this was spoken at the same time as the message to the ambassadors.

Matthew Henry sets out the situation the counsel answers. Judah and Jerusalem had often contested with the king of Babylon and always been worsted; many of their valuable persons and goods were carried there already, including some vessels of the Lord’s house, and the question was how the struggle would end. They had men pretending to be prophets who bade them hold out, promising they would soon be too hard for the king and recover all they had lost; the prophet is sent to bid them yield, since instead of recovering what was lost they would otherwise lose all that remained. Henry finds the counsel remarkable for what it asks: is it their wisdom to submit to the heavy iron yoke of a cruel tyrant in order to secure the lives of their bodies? and is it not much more our wisdom to submit to the sweet and easy yoke of our rightful Lord, in order to secure the lives of our souls? Bring down your spirits to repentance and faith, he says, and that is the way to bring up your spirits to heaven.

The alternative is stated as a question rather than a threat. Calvin observes that all means were used not only to invite the Jews but to stimulate them: pardon was offered if they quietly submitted to be chastised; and because they could not be sufficiently moved by that kindness, the warning is added that unless they receive the life offered them they must inevitably perish. Nothing was left undone to bend them to obedience, and by naming the three judgments the prophet intimates that there would be no end until they were consumed, unless they suffered themselves to be chastised by a paternal kindness that would prove salutary. Adam Clarke puts the alternative in a sentence: if they resist the king to whom the commission has been given they shall be destroyed by sword and famine; if they submit they shall escape all these evils. Gill glosses the death threatened as coming through the blockade of an invading army upon a refusal to bear the yoke. On the prophets who told them otherwise, Gill remarks that such kings always had such men about them, to whom they listened, often to bad consequence; Keil and Delitzsch keep to the terms of the warning, that these men were not sent and prophesy falsely in God’s name, so that people and prophets perish together.
15:
The charge against the false prophets is not merely that they were wrong but that they used the divine name, and John Gill weighs the aggravation: to deliver a lie was wicked in itself and fatal to others, but to cover it with the name of the Lord and back it with his authority was much more abominable. John Calvin makes the verse a lesson in discrimination. The object is to show that the Jews were not to receive thoughtlessly everything presented under God’s name but to exercise judgment; and he calls this worthy of special notice, since the devil has ever falsely assumed that name, and every delusion that has prevailed in the world has obtained credit by no other pretence. Many in his own day are wilfully blind, thinking themselves excused if they can plead ignorance and protesting that they dare not make curious inquiries; and since many willingly put on nooses and wish to be deceived, the rule is to be noticed, that we must distinguish true prophets from false and depend only on those God has sent. He then explains where the difference lay. Prophets had to be raised up in a special manner, since to predict hidden events was a special gift, so that the office was not an ordinary one like the priesthood; the promise of a prophet raised from among their brethren stood always in force, yet none was to take the office unless endowed with an extraordinary gift, and being a priest did not qualify a man for it.

The message is then carried from the court to the temple. Gill describes the move: the prophet spoke to the priests ministering there and to the people assembled for worship, a proper time and place to meet them, since the priests especially had a concern in what he had to say about the vessels. Calvin explains why the king was addressed first and the priests and people only now. It was necessary to begin with the king, since earthly kings think much of their dignity and the people depend on their will—an earlier prophet condemned them for rendering too willing an obedience to royal edicts and worshipping God as the king dictated—and since the royal name dazzled the eyes of the simple, the prophet addressed him first. But the priests, Calvin says, were included, and their case was monstrous: designed to be interpreters of the law and honoured by the saying that the priest’s lips should keep knowledge and that from him the law is to be sought, they were nonetheless so stupid as to receive along with the common people whatever they heard from the false prophets, and did not distinguish truth from falsehood.

The particular prediction at issue is the return of the temple vessels, and Charles Ellicott explains why so much was staked on it. The vessels were those carried off in the first invasion, before Zedekiah’s accession; the people mourned the absence of what they had prized among the treasures of the temple, and the prophets accordingly soothed them with predictions that they would soon be brought back. In marked contrast to those promises of a speedy restoration, he notes, the vessels appear in use at a Babylonian feast towards the close of the exile and are restored only by Cyrus after the capture of Babylon. He records a tradition in an apocryphal book that some of them, silver and not gold, were restored in Zedekiah’s reign, but thinks it hardly historical, and observes that the narrative connects the restoration with the prophet’s own secretary, who would scarcely have fulfilled a prediction made by his master’s enemies. Adam Clarke is blunter, calling the prediction simply a lie: the vessels were not to be restored until God brought them up, which was after the captivity when they were sent back by the same king.
17:
The same counsel is repeated, and John Calvin explains the repetition as a necessity of controversy. With no adversary opposing him a man may deal calmly with the teachable and confine himself to a few words; but when opponents appear who seek to subvert what he says, those driven different ways will not be satisfied with a few. Seeing the people fluctuating, the prophet used many words to confirm them—not that prolixity convinces, but he spoke efficiently enough to influence some. Besides, the subject was not plausible: the false prophets were heard with favour, since the hope of impunity is always sought after by the world, whereas this counsel was a very hard speech. Subjection carried reproach; they were bidden to surrender to a most cruel enemy and to risk being spoiled of all they had. Charles Ellicott shows why the rival prediction had to be met: the promised restoration of the vessels was not a mere forecast but an incentive to rebellion—make one last effort, the prophets virtually said, and the spoiler shall be compelled to disgorge his booty—while the prophet saw that such an effort would only hasten the destruction of temple and city.

The challenge that follows is the sharpest thing in the chapter. Ellicott sets out the wager on each side: the rival prophets had staked their credit on the return of the vessels already taken, and the prophet stakes his on the prediction that what was spared in the first invasion would be taken in the second; they had better use their gift of the Spirit, if any, in interceding for what remained. Calvin hears the same irony. The prophet laughs to scorn the confidence with which the false prophets were swollen, and says that instead of the prosperity they promised they ought to have dreaded a grievous punishment; comparing the future with the past, he shows that these impostors promised a better state of things when heavy judgment was impending and both city and temple doomed to ruin. He examines the verb rendered make intercession, noting that it properly means to meet or go to meet and is used metaphorically of interceding, since one who meets another as intercessor in a manner restrains the opponent; two ancient versions give only the first sense and so convey no meaning, a third renders it simply pray. From the passage, he adds, teaching and praying are united, God requiring the man he sets as a teacher to be assiduous in prayer. John Gill makes the same test the mark of a true prophet, that such are sent by God and have his word put into them.

The inventory is identified item by item. Adam Clarke describes the two brazen columns in the portico, eighteen cubits high and twelve in circumference, and the brazen sea, ten cubits across, which held water for the washings and stood on twelve brazen oxen. Ellicott identifies the bases as the ten stands for the lavers with their engraved work of cherubim, lions and palm-trees, observes that the plunder had apparently been confined at first to the more portable vessels, cups and flagons and the like, and notes that the absence of the list from the Greek version has led some critics to conclude it was a later addition to the Hebrew text. Calvin explains the enumeration: the conqueror had in part spared the temple and city, taking chiefly the precious vessels, so that since some splendour remained the Jews ought to have learned that he had acted kindly; now they are told nothing will remain. Gill names the two pillars, and Matthew Henry sums the sentence up—the brazen vessels shall go after the golden ones—while noting that the passage ends with a gracious promise of their return, so that though the recovery of the church’s prosperity does not come in our time we must not despair, since it will come in God’s.
20:
The reminder of what was left behind is turned into a charge of ingratitude. John Calvin puts the argument at length. The Jews did not acknowledge that the cruelty of their enemy had been moderated by divine power; the Babylonians were cruel and their avarice insatiable, and nothing would have been left in the temple had not their hands been in a manner restrained by the hidden power of God. The prophet alludes to that ingratitude in observing that the conqueror had not taken these vessels even when he carried away the king and all the chief men of the city and the land. Calvin makes the comparison explicit: he would not have been so gentle had not God moderated his spirit, for he spared not their king and led all their chief men into exile; how then was it that anything was left in the city and the pillars were not taken? Did he despise them, polished with exquisite skill and made of costly material? They ought to have seen a proof of mercy in what still remained safe in the city and the temple, and yet they disregarded so great a benefit—what then must at length happen to them? He draws a general lesson from it, that whenever God chastises us we should consider what has been spared. John Gill supplies the factual basis, that the conqueror seems to have taken only the vessels of gold and to have left those of brass.

The repetition in the next verse is deliberate, and Calvin explains why. The prophet emphatically expresses what was of itself clear enough, in order to imprint the declaration deeply on their minds, so that some terror might penetrate hearts so obdurate that a simple statement of the truth could effect nothing. He also settles a small point of grammar, holding that the particle opening the verse must here be affirmative rather than causal, and noting that all the versions but one keep the causal sense. He then weighs an ambiguous pronoun in the promise of a visitation. It may refer to the vessels, which suits the reference well enough; but since Hebrew often uses a pronoun without any preceding noun when something remarkable is spoken of, he inclines to refer it to the Jews themselves, since the restoration of the vessels depended on the restoration of the people. The vessels, on that reading, would be held captive until God allowed the people a free return, which happened by the edict of the Persian king after he obtained power; and the Jews are reminded that the exile foretold would be long, and that they hoped foolishly for what the false prophets had promised about the vessels, since God had no greater care for the vessels than for his chosen people, the vessels being acceptable to him for the people’s sake.

The chapter closes on a date that is not given. Charles Ellicott notes that the fulfilment of the prediction is recorded in the history, and that the time is left indefinite, though seventy years had already been named elsewhere as the period between the plunder and the restoration. He hears a deliberate contrast in the phrasing: the undefined vagueness of the day that I will visit them is set against the equally indefinite but far more exciting shortly of the false prophets. Adam Clarke states the alternative the chapter has been pressing throughout, that so far from those already taken being brought back, those which now remain shall be carried after them unless the people submit; they did not submit, he adds, and the prophecy was literally fulfilled. Gill notes only that the vessels were carried there as foretold, and that a particular account of them is given elsewhere in the book.
